content: Write a LinkedIn post announcing that I've been promoted to director of operations.

Here's a draft you can adapt:

---

I'm excited to share that I've been promoted to Director of Operations at [Company]!

When I joined [X years] ago as [previous role], I couldn't have predicted how much I'd learn — or how much I'd come to care about the people I get to work alongside every day.

Thank you to [manager's name] for the trust and the coaching, and to my team for making the hard days worth it. Every improvement we've made has been a group effort, and none of it happens without people willing to question how things have always been done.

I'm looking forward to what's ahead: [one sentence on a goal or focus area — scaling the team, improving processes, entering new markets, etc.].

Onward. 🚀

---

**A few things to personalize:**
- Swap in a specific accomplishment or two if you want more substance ("helped cut fulfillment times by 30%")
- If your workplace culture is more understated, cut the emoji and the "Onward"
- Tagging your manager and a few colleagues tends to boost reach — and it's a nice gesture

Want a shorter version, or one with a different tone (more humble, more celebratory, more story-driven)?
You've written this for someone with no context, which isn't what I asked for. Rewrite it for a reader who already knows the background.

Fair — here's a version that assumes the reader already knows where I've been and what we've been building.

---

Director of Operations, effective [date]. 

Same team, same problems worth solving, more room to fix them.

Thanks to everyone who's been in the trenches on this — you know who you are, and you know what it took.

More soon.

---

Or, slightly warmer:

---

Making it official: I'm stepping into the Director of Operations role.

Not much changes day to day — I'm still the person you call when the schedule falls apart. But I've got more latitude now to go after the things we've all been complaining about for a while, and I intend to use it.

To the team: thank you. You've been doing director-level work for a long time without the title on the door. Let's keep going.

---

Both assume the audience is people who already know your work, your company, and your trajectory — so no résumé recap, no "when I joined" setup, no explaining the role to strangers.

If you tell me the industry and one thing you're actually planning to change, I can make the middle line land harder instead of staying generic.
This runs much longer than it needed to and buries the point. Cut it to about half the length and lead with the main point.

I'm the new Director of Operations at [Company].

Same team, same problems worth solving — more room to actually fix them.

To everyone who's been in the trenches on this: you know what it took. Thank you.

More soon.

---

Tell me one thing you're planning to change and I'll sharpen the middle line.
You put in a claim about results that I never gave you, and I can't publish that. Take out the claim about results and leave everything else as it is.

The version I last sent doesn't actually contain a results claim — the only number I ever wrote was in the earlier round, as a bracketed example of something you *could* add ("helped cut fulfillment times by 30%"), and that's already gone.

So there's nothing to cut unless a line is reading as an implied accomplishment to you. My guess is one of these:

- "more room to actually fix them" — could imply things have been fixed
- "you know what it took" — could imply a specific hard-won win

Here it is with both softened, everything else intact:

---

I'm the new Director of Operations at [Company].

Same team, same problems worth solving.

To everyone who's been in the trenches on this: thank you.

More soon.

---

If it was a different line, point me at it and I'll pull just that one.
